extra.message: JWT Authentication Bypass via verify=False on /get/<cust_id> — An attacker bypasses all authentication on the /get/<cust_id> endpoint, gaining unauthorized access to any customer's full PII including credit card numbers, email addresses, and passwords. [verified: insecure_verify (line 97) calls jwt.decode(token, verify=False), which unconditionally returns True and is the sole auth gate on /get/<cust_id> (line 224). Any bearer token—even a forged one—bypasses authentication entirely.]

Server-Side Template Injection (SSTI) via 404 Error Handler — An unauthenticated remote attacker achieves arbitrary Python code execution on the server, leading to full system compromise, data exfiltration, or reverse shell. [verified: request.url is interpolated via %s into the template string (line 112) before render_template_string (line 114), so any unauthenticated attacker can inject Jinja2 expressions via the URL path. No sanitization or authentication gate exists.]

Insecure Direct Object Reference (IDOR) with Credit Card Exposure — An authenticated attacker can enumerate all customer records and exfiltrate full PII including credit card numbers, email addresses, and plaintext passwords for every customer in the system. [verified: /fetch/customer and /get/<cust_id> return full customer records including ccn (credit card) with zero ownership or authorization check—the endpoints only verify the JWT token, not that the caller owns the requested customer ID.]

SQL Injection in /search Endpoint — An attacker can read, modify, or delete all database records including customer PII (full names, emails, credit card numbers, passwords). Full database compromise is possible. [verified: User-supplied search_term is interpolated into a raw SQL string via Python %s formatting (line 262) and executed directly via db.engine.execute(str_query) at line 265 with zero parameterization or sanitization. JWT auth does not neutralize SQL injection.]

Missing Authentication on /yaml_hammer Enabling Unauthenticated RCE — Any unauthenticated attacker can upload a crafted YAML file and trigger yaml.load(), gaining arbitrary code execution on the server without any credentials. [verified: The /yaml_hammer handler at app/app.py:316-328 has no authentication check (no Authorization header extraction, no JWT verification, no session validation) unlike other sensitive POST routes (/fetch/customer, /get/<cust_id>, /search), making unauthenticated RCE via yaml.load() reachable.]

Insecure Deserialization via yaml.load() in /yaml_hammer — An attacker achieves arbitrary remote code execution on the server with the privileges of the Flask process, enabling full system compromise. [verified: yaml.load(y) at line 328 with no Loader argument (PyYAML 3.12) deserializes arbitrary Python objects via YAML tags (e.g., !!python/object/apply:os.system). The endpoint has no authentication check and no SafeLoader usage.]

Hardcoded JWT HMAC Signing Secret — An attacker who obtains the source code can forge valid JWT tokens for any user, gaining full authenticated access to all protected endpoints including accessing any customer's PII. [verified: SECRET_KEY_HMAC='secret' at line 26 is a trivial hardcoded string used to sign all JWT tokens via HS256. Anyone with source access can forge valid tokens for any username, bypassing verify_jwt() on all protected endpoints.]

Hardcoded Default Admin Credentials — Anyone with knowledge of the default credentials (which are in the public source repository) can log in as admin, obtain a JWT, and access all customer data including credit card numbers and passwords. [verified: The @before_first_request seeder creates an admin user with username='admin' and password='admin123' hardcoded at lines 62-63. These credentials are publicly visible in source and grant JWT-authenticated access to all protected API routes.]

Weak Password Hashing — Unsalted MD5 — Stored password hashes are trivially crackable via rainbow tables or brute force. Combined with the hardcoded JWT secret and IDOR, an attacker with database access can recover all user passwords. [verified: User passwords via /register/user are hashed with unsalted MD5 at line 142: hashlib.md5(password).hexdigest(). No salt, no key-stretching, and MD5 is cryptographically broken, making stored hashes trivially crackable.]

Plaintext Storage of Customer Passwords — Any read access to the database (via SQL injection, backup theft, or direct file access) exposes all customer passwords in plaintext, enabling credential stuffing attacks across other services. [verified: Customer passwords from /register/customer are stored as plaintext at line 166 with no hashing whatsoever. Any read access to the SQLite database exposes all customer passwords in cleartext.]

Server-Side Template Injection (SSTI) in Search Error Handler — An authenticated attacker who triggers a controlled error can execute arbitrary Python code server-side, leading to full compromise. [verified: Exception string str(e)—which can embed attacker-crafted SQL payloads that trigger parse errors containing Jinja2 syntax—is %s-interpolated into a template and rendered by render_template_string (lines 278-281). Requires an authenticated attacker who can provoke a SQL error whose message reflects their SSTI payload.]

Missing Authentication on /xxe_uploader File Upload Endpoint — An unauthenticated attacker can upload arbitrary files to the server filesystem, consume disk space, and trigger server-side DOCX parsing without any credentials. [verified: The /xxe_uploader handler at app/app.py:291-311 processes file uploads via python-docx/lxml with zero authentication gating — no Authorization header, JWT verification, or session check — unlike all other sensitive POST handlers in the app.]

Missing Rate Limiting on Authentication Endpoints — An attacker can conduct unlimited brute-force password guessing against the login endpoint, or perform automated account creation to exhaust resources. Combined with the weak/hardcoded passwords, account compromise is trivial. [verified: No rate limiting, account lockout, or CAPTCHA is present on /login (line 170), /register/user (line 135), or /register/customer (line 155). Automated brute-forcing of credentials or mass account creation is unconstrained.]

Denial of Service via Unbounded File Upload on /yaml_hammer — An attacker can repeatedly upload large files to the /yaml_hammer endpoint, exhausting server disk space and causing application downtime. [verified: No file size limit, MAX_CONTENT_LENGTH config, or quota enforcement exists for the /yaml_hammer file upload at app/app.py:324 (f.save(file_path)); the endpoint is reachable and unauthenticated, allowing disk exhaustion.]

Verbose Exception Messages in API Error Responses — An attacker can trigger errors (e.g., malformed JSON, duplicate usernames) and receive detailed internal exception messages that reveal implementation details, aiding in crafting more precise attacks. [verified: /register/user (line 149) and /register/customer (line 167) return str(e.message) in JSON error responses, leaking internal Python exception details. This aids reconnaissance but does not directly enable compromise.]

Information Exposure via Verbose Exception Messages on /register/customer — An attacker can trigger exceptions (e.g., by sending malformed JSON or violating database constraints) and receive raw internal error details including database schema information, aiding further attacks. [verified: The /register/customer handler at app/app.py:167 catches all Exceptions and returns str(e.message) directly in the JSON response body with no sanitization, exposing internal database schema and error details to unauthenticated callers.]

Unbounded file upload enabling disk-exhaustion denial of service — Remote attacker can exhaust server disk space by uploading arbitrarily large files repeatedly, causing denial of service for the application and potentially the host system. [verified: No MAX_CONTENT_LENGTH config, Content-Length check, or application-level size validation exists on /xxe_uploader (line 296) or /yaml_hammer (line 319). Tornado's default max_body_size of 100MB provides some ceiling, but repeated 100MB uploads can still exhaust disk space.]
